cards.front: What does Big O notation describe?
cards.back: How the number of operations, or the resources needed, grow as the size of the input grows. It describes the worst case and ignores constant factors and lower-order terms.

keyPoints.text: how resource use grows with input size

cards.explanation: Ignoring constants is what makes Big O a statement about growth rather than about a particular machine or implementation.

cards.front: Order these from slowest growing to fastest: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), O(2^n).
cards.back: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), O(2^n).

keyPoints.text: then n log n then n squared then exponential

cards.explanation: The gap between O(n log n) and O(n^2) is what makes the choice of sorting algorithm matter for large data sets.

cards.front: What is the time complexity of two nested loops that each run n times?
cards.explanation: The inner loop body runs n times for each of the n outer iterations, so n x n = n^2 operations. O(2n) is just O(n), which is the trap here.

cards.front: Why does Big O ignore constant factors such as the 2 in 2n?
cards.back: Because it describes how quickly running time grows as the input becomes large, and multiplying by a constant does not change that growth rate: 2n and n both double when n doubles, so they are the same class.

keyPoints.text: it describes growth rate for large inputs
a constant multiple does not change the growth rate
synonyms: 2n and n are the same class

cards.explanation: This is why an O(n) algorithm with a large constant will eventually beat an O(n^2) algorithm with a small one, even if it is slower on small inputs.

cards.front: An O(n log n) algorithm takes 2 seconds for n = 1000. Estimate how long it takes for n = 2000, using log base 2.
cards.explanation: Doubling n doubles the n factor and adds one to log2 n, from about 10 to about 11, so the work grows by a factor of about 2.2 and 2 s becomes roughly 4.4 s. The 4.0 s answer treats it as plain O(n).

cards.front: What is the time complexity of `while n > 1: n = n // 2`?

keyPoints.text: n is halved on every iteration
synonyms: the problem size halves each time

cards.explanation: Each iteration halves $n$, so after $k$ iterations the value is $\frac{n}{2^k}$. Reaching 1 needs $k = \log_2 n$ iterations. Halving is the signature of logarithmic complexity and is the same reason binary search is so efficient. Doubling $n$ adds only one more iteration, which is the practical meaning of $O(\log n)$.

cards.front: An $O(n^2)$ algorithm takes 3 seconds when $n = 500$. Estimate the time when $n = 2500$.

keyPoints.text: quadratic means the time rises by a factor of 25

cards.explanation: The input grows by a factor of 5, and a quadratic algorithm's work grows by $5^2 = 25$, so $3 \times 25 = 75$ seconds. The answer 15 seconds applies the factor once, which would be right for a linear algorithm. This scaling is the practical reason quadratic sorts are unusable on large data: a hundredfold increase in size means a ten-thousandfold increase in time.

cards.front: State the best, worst and average case complexities of linear search and of binary search on $n$ items.
cards.back: Linear search: best $O(1)$, worst and average $O(n)$. Binary search: best $O(1)$, worst and average $O(\log n)$.

keyPoints.text: linear search best case is O(1)
linear search worst case is O(n)
synonyms: the item is last or absent

keyPoints.text: binary search worst case is O(log n)

distractors: Linear: $O(n)$ in every case. Binary: $O(\log n)$ in every case

cards.explanation: The best case is $O(1)$ for both, since either can find the item on the first comparison. What separates them is the worst case: linear search may examine every item, while binary search halves the remaining range each time. Quoting only one figure per algorithm is the common way to lose this mark - the three cases are genuinely different for linear search.

cards.front: What is space complexity, and how does it differ from time complexity?
cards.back: Space complexity measures the extra memory an algorithm needs beyond its input, as a function of input size. It is a separate resource: an algorithm can trade one against the other.

synonyms: memory used as a function of input size

keyPoints.text: time and space can be traded off
synonyms: using more memory can save time

mcq.correct: Extra memory needed, traded against time
distractors: The size of the input file on disk
The number of variables declared in the source code
Total memory including the input and the program

cards.explanation: Merge sort is the standard example of the trade-off: it sorts in $O(n \log n)$ time but needs $O(n)$ extra memory for the merged halves, where insertion sort is in-place with $O(1)$ extra space but quadratic time. Counting the input itself is not usual - space complexity means the additional working memory.

cards.front: What is the time complexity of a naive recursive Fibonacci function with no memoisation, and why?
cards.back: $O(2^n)$, because each call branches into two further calls and the same subproblems are recomputed many times.

keyPoints.text: each call makes two recursive calls
synonyms: the call tree doubles at each level

cards.explanation: The call tree has roughly $2^n$ nodes: computing fib(5) makes 15 calls in total, of which fib(3) is computed twice and fib(2) three times. Storing each result the first time it is found reduces this to $O(n)$, which is exactly what memoisation buys. Exponential growth is why this function is unusable beyond about $n = 40$ despite the task being trivial.

cards.front: Why can an $O(n \log n)$ algorithm be slower in practice than an $O(n^2)$ one for small inputs?
cards.back: Because Big O hides constant factors. For small $n$ a low-constant quadratic algorithm can do less actual work than a high-constant $n \log n$ one.

keyPoints.text: for small n the crossover has not happened yet
synonyms: the asymptotic advantage has not kicked in
insertion sort beats merge sort on short lists

mcq.correct: Big O hides constant factors, which dominate for small $n$
distractors: Because $O(n^2)$ is actually smaller than $O(n \log n)$ for small $n$
Because Big O only describes worst-case behaviour

cards.explanation: Big O describes growth as $n \to \infty$ and discards both constant factors and lower-order terms. An $O(n^2)$ algorithm doing $n^2$ simple operations beats an $O(n \log n)$ algorithm doing $100 n \log n$ until $n$ is around $2^{100}$, which never happens. This is why real sorting libraries use insertion sort for short sublists and switch to merge or quick sort for longer ones.

cards.front:
What is the time complexity of this pseudocode?
```
for i <- 1 to n
  for j <- 1 to i
    total <- total + a[j]
```
cards.back: $O(n^2)$, because the inner loop runs $i$ times so the total work is $1 + 2 + \ldots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

keyPoints.text: the inner loop runs i times, not n
synonyms: the inner bound depends on the outer variable

distractors: $O(n^2 \log n)$: two nested loops with a sum

cards.explanation: The inner loop runs $1 + 2 + \ldots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ times in total, which is $\frac{1}{2}n^2 + \frac{1}{2}n$. Dropping the constant and the lower-order term leaves $O(n^2)$. The halving of the average inner length is real but only affects the hidden constant, not the class - a trap worth remembering whenever the inner bound depends on the outer variable.
